item.research_question: How can a high-entropy alloy (VZrHfNbTa) be modified with a hafnium coating via hot-press sintering to improve its ultra-high temperature oxidation resistance and bonding mechanism?
item.material_system: VZrHfNbTa High-Entropy Alloy (HEA) substrate coated with Hafnium (Hf) powder
item.processing_route: Embedding hot-press method: VZrHfNbTa powder compressed at 4 MPa into 8 mm cylinder; Hf powder laid on graphite mold; pressed at 1823 K (1550 °C) with 30 MPa pressure for 1 h; cooling rate 12.4 K/min
item.test_conditions: Isothermal oxidation in air at 1873 K (1600 °C) for 5 h; surface hardness measured before and after oxidation
key_findings: Coating thickness of the composite is about 120 μm
Diffusion distance of zirconium in the hafnium coating is about 60 μm
Weight gain of coated sample after oxidation is 56.56 mg/cm²
Weight gain of uncoated sample is 98.09 mg/cm² (coated is 57.7% of uncoated)
Surface hardness of coated specimen decreased by 8.995% (from 1612 HV to 1467 HV)
Surface hardness of uncoated specimen decreased by 57.562% (from 1534 HV to 651 HV)
HfC surface layer thickness is less than 10 μm
item.mechanism: Zirconium from the substrate diffuses into the hafnium coating to form an HfZr alloy transition layer that chemically bonds the coating and substrate. During oxidation, the hafnium coating forms a dense HfO2 protective layer that prevents deep oxidation. Lattice distortion in the Hf-Zr solid solution promotes zirconium diffusion, enhancing adhesion and preventing peeling.
item.limitations: The text notes that individual areas of hafnium powder were not covered enough in some regions, leading to pits, and that cracks appeared on the coating surface due to sintering volume shrinkage of high melting point HfC.
item.future_work: The authors state the study aims to 'establish an experimental foundation for subsequent research' and provide a 'research basis for the study of high-temperature resistant composites.'
quotes: The results show that zirconium in the matrix will diffuse into the hafnium coating during the high-temperature sintering process and form the HfZr alloy transition layer
The weight gain of the coated sample after oxidation is 56.56 mg/cm2, which is only 57.7% compared to the weight gain of the uncoated sample
The migration of zirconium element at the interface between the coating and the substrate helps to improve the binding force between the coating and the substrate

records.text: Paper card. Question: How can a high-entropy alloy (VZrHfNbTa) be modified with a hafnium coating via hot-press sintering to improve its ultra-high temperature oxidation resistance and bonding mechanism?. System: VZrHfNbTa High-Entropy Alloy (HEA) substrate coated with Hafnium (Hf) powder. Processing: Embedding hot-press method: VZrHfNbTa powder compressed at 4 MPa into 8 mm cylinder; Hf powder laid on graphite mold; pressed at 1823 K (1550 °C) with 30 MPa pressure for 1 h; cooling rate 12.4 K/min. Test conditions: Isothermal oxidation in air at 1873 K (1600 °C) for 5 h; surface hardness measured before and after oxidation. Findings: Coating thickness of the composite is about 120 μm; Diffusion distance of zirconium in the hafnium coating is about 60 μm; Weight gain of coated sample after oxidation is 56.56 mg/cm²; Weight gain of uncoated sample is 98.09 mg/cm² (coated is 57.7% of uncoated); Surface hardness of coated specimen decreased by 8.995% (from 1612 HV to 1467 HV); Surface hardness of uncoated specimen decreased by 57.562% (from 1534 HV to 651 HV); HfC surface layer thickness is less than 10 μm. Mechanism: Zirconium from the substrate diffuses into the hafnium coating to form an HfZr alloy transition layer that chemically bonds the coating and substrate. During oxidation, the hafnium coating forms a dense HfO2 protective layer that prevents deep oxidation. Lattice distortion in the Hf-Zr solid solution promotes zirconium diffusion, enhancing adhesion and preventing peeling.. Limitations: The text notes that individual areas of hafnium powder were not covered enough in some regions, leading to pits, and that cracks appeared on the coating surface due to sintering volume shrinkage of high melting point HfC.. Future work: The authors state the study aims to 'establish an experimental foundation for subsequent research' and provide a 'research basis for the study of high-temperature resistant composites.'. Quote: "The results show that zirconium in the matrix will diffuse into the hafnium coating during the high-temperature sintering process and form the HfZr alloy transition layer"
